claimed.text: At the National Press Club on 27 September 2010, which CNN streamed, Hastings presented seven Air Force veterans: Dwynne Arneson, Bruce Fenstermacher, Charles Halt, Robert Jamison, Patrick McDonough, Jerry Nelson and Robert Salas. From the podium he said that, in his and their opinion, whoever was aboard the craft was sending a signal to Washington and Moscow "that we are playing with fire".

Each panellist's post is given in his own affidavit or on Hastings's page: Arneson with the 28th Air Division at Malmstrom in 1967, Fenstermacher a missile combat crew commander at Warren from 1974 to 1977, McDonough a geodetic surveyor out of Warren from 1962 to 1966, Nelson a deputy missile crew commander at Walker AFB, Roswell, from 1962 to 1965, and Jamison an ICBM targeting team commander at Malmstrom. For Fenstermacher, McDonough and Arneson the bases and dates are their own, as published by Hastings, and no service record has been opened.

How the panel reached us: Halt had written the operative document himself in 1981 as a serving deputy base commander, and Salas approached a newspaper himself in 1996, but for Arneson, Fenstermacher, McDonough, Nelson and Jamison no dated public statement before Hastings's 2010 event has been found.
Arneson is reported as relaying a remark by the Boeing engineer Robert Kaminski that the Echo Flight missiles were perfect and clean; the board carries it at Tier 3, as a relayed remark.
Hastings says he holds signed affidavits from Salas, Halt, McDonough, Jamison, Arneson, Fenstermacher and Nelson, published in facsimile in his archive.

The Malmstrom corroboration reached the public through the interviewer or the claimant: Walter Figel as Hastings's recordings of three calls, Frederick Meiwald as a letter to Salas and Hastings's recorded calls, Jamison as the source of the date Hastings uses, and Kaminski as a 1997 letter to a researcher that Hastings publishes.

Other routes into the register run the opposite way. Salas approached the Great Falls Tribune himself; Runyon contacted the Center for UFO Studies on his own initiative in 2000; the Warren reports became public because Blue Book's consultant printed its telephone log. At Ellsworth, Mario Woods had told his account under his own name since 1996, while Michael Johnson was found by the party publishing the result.
On the board's reading, Hastings extended the documentary method of Clear Intent by pairing FOIA paper with signed affidavits from named officers.

contested.text: The size and make-up of the witness population is not stable. Hastings's press-conference page says more than 160 veterans, his biography more than 150; Jesse Michels gave 167 and then almost 200, and later said Hastings had corrected him, with only about 12 to 15 radar operators and the rest ICBM security personnel.

Hastings's method of finding witnesses is not stated on any page the board has opened, so every node whose sole source is a Hastings interview carries the note that the route by which the witness was found is undocumented.

The Malmstrom corroboration is circular on the board's reading: four witnesses who share a single interviewer are one method applied four times. The separation of Oscar Flight from Echo Flight, which lets the Oscar claim survive the unit history's silence, was made by the same interviewer on a witness he interviewed.

The claim that the Personnel Reliability Program kept nuclear-site personnel from reporting what they saw, repeated on the American Alchemy programme with a figure of 167 attached, is unsupported: the 167 is Hastings's witness count, and the directive contains no provision about reporting aerial phenomena.

The record against the Malmstrom accounts: the Air Force history says the UFO rumours were disproven, Echo Flight's crew commander Eric Carlson says no UFO-related call reached him, and his son James Carlson has published a sustained case that no UFOs were involved at any flight; on the number of missiles, though, the same history supports Salas's ten against the three or four attributed to Eric Carlson.
The affidavit list does not agree with itself: Hastings's archive lists Nelson among the affiants, while his press-conference page names six affiants and not Nelson.

The individual Malmstrom corroborations are each disputed: James Carlson says Figel told him he saw no UFO and treated the radio report as a joke; Tim Hebert says Figel's two Hastings interviews contradict each other and that Figel declined to sign an affidavit; Meiwald's 1996 letter is characterised in two incompatible ways; and the Air Force history contradicts Kaminski's claim that the inquiry was stopped with no report.

record.text: The board opened and read two document sets Hastings relies on, the 341st Strategic Missile Wing histories and the 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log for November 1975, and found them saying what he says they say; the F. E. Warren Blue Book telephone log of 1 August 1965 was read only through a mirror of Hastings's own material.

Hastings publishes the primary documents under his cases, including FBI memoranda on Los Alamos of December 1948 and on Los Alamos and Sandia of August 1950, Warren documents of 1 August 1965, Minot documents of 1966, an Air Force teletype of 17 March 1967 on loss of strategic alert, and 1975 Malmstrom material.

The Personnel Reliability Program directive, DoD Directive 5210.42 in its 25 May 1993 edition, applies to military, civilian and contractor personnel in nuclear weapons duties. It lets demeanour disqualify, listing aberrant attitude, behaviour or mood; opens medical records to certifying officials without the person's consent; and runs on self-reporting and peer review.

SAC is the reporting node in the primary records: the NMCC memorandum of 29 October 1975 records NORAD informed by SAC, the 24th NORAD Region log is largely a record of calls from SAC command posts, and the 341st wing history records SAC Headquarters calling in engineering support within hours of the Echo Flight shutdown on 16 March 1967.

The Air Force's own wing history records the Echo Flight shutdown and states that rumours of UFOs around the flight were disproven, on the evidence of a team that had been at November Flight; the strings Oscar, O Flight, 24 Mar and 25 Mar do not occur in the released pages, which the covering letter describes as excerpts.
The 1968 Minot debriefing record names Capt. Bradford Runyon as the B-52 co-pilot, which puts his presence in a contemporaneous Air Force file.
Fawcett and Greenwood's Clear Intent of 1984 is built on documents obtained under FOIA from the CIA, FBI, NSA, Air Force, NORAD and the Joint Chiefs, reproduced and annotated.

summary.text: Hastings's output has two halves that the board grades differently: the documents he relies on and republishes, two sets of which the board opened independently and found to say what he says, and the interviews, whose route to the public is often undocumented.

The witnesses sit inside one institutional frame: the Minuteman bases at Malmstrom and Warren were Strategic Air Command installations, SAC appears as the reporting chain in the primary records, and a Personnel Reliability Program directive, in an edition of 1993 reissuing one of 1985, now sets the rules for personnel in nuclear weapons duties.

Against the interview-led cases the board sets control cases that reached the record by other routes: a Minot B-52 co-pilot who approached a research body himself, and a Warren telephone log printed by Project Blue Book's own consultant.

On the board's reading, Richard Dolan's institutional history supplies the frame in which Hastings's casework sits: concealment argued from the documented secrecy architecture, with the nuclear complex as the place where compartment density and incident documentation coincide.

title: UFOs and nuclear weapons: the witness register
